method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The Federal Reserve kept rates at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday, with two officials voting for a hike, and Chair Kevin Warsh made no promise on December, so the dollar slipped from its two-week high. It held steady in Asia on Thursday as a tech-share slide kept buyers cautious; Thursday's US growth and inflation figures come next.

EUR.text: The euro is near $1.113, close to its lowest since May 2025, as France's budget strain keeps its borrowing costs high. The European Central Bank decides on Thursday, October 29, and is expected to hold at 2.5%; markets still expect more hikes, so a firm hint about December could lift the euro, while worry about France or talk of Christine Lagarde leaving early could weigh.

GBP.text: Chancellor John Healey's first budget left £15 billion of spare room and passed without a bond-market scare: UK borrowing costs fell and shares rose. The pound still slipped to about $1.33 against a strong dollar; the Bank of England decision on November 5, where a hike is likely, is what could move it next.

JPY.text: The yen is weak near 158 per dollar because Japan's rates are far below US rates. But a Bank of Japan gauge of underlying inflation just hit a three-year high, which, with Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama's warnings that Tokyo may step in, slows the fall; the bank decides on Friday and is expected to hold at 1.25% while hinting at a December hike.

CHF.text: The franc is near a three-month high against the euro after last week's rush to shelter. Monday's talks in Tehran ended with a promise to keep talking, and French bond markets calmed, which takes some of that demand away.

CAD.text: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% on Wednesday, its first hike in three years, and said more may be needed. The Canadian dollar firmed late in the day as the US dollar softened after the Fed and Canadian yields rose; oil above $100, a big Canadian export, adds some support.

AUD.text: Australian inflation came in hotter than the Reserve Bank of Australia forecast, and Governor Michele Bullock said the board will ask next week whether four hikes this year are enough. With New Zealand's central bank pausing, the Australian dollar rose to its strongest against the kiwi in over a decade.

NZD.text: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand kept its rate at 2.75% on Wednesday, October 28, when nearly everyone expected a rise to 3%, and the kiwi fell about 1.7% to roughly 55.9 US cents. The bank still says more hikes are likely, but not yet, so the kiwi has lost its rate support for now.

XAU.text: Gold is near $4,050 and down about 2.5% in October, held back by a likely US rate hike in December, which weighs on a metal that pays no interest. Central-bank buying gives it a floor, and mixed signals on US-Iran talks keep some demand for shelter alive; a soft US inflation reading on Thursday would give it some relief.

OIL.text: Brent crude is near $114, still far above $100, because the Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut and Yemen's Houthi rebels keep firing at Saudi Arabia. It slipped on Thursday as Qatar offered Iran a new draft deal and Vice President JD Vance reportedly wrote to Tehran about talks, but fresh tanker hits and fear of US strikes after the November 3 midterms keep the war premium in place.

items.headline: Asian Shares Slide as Alphabet Earnings Miss, Wall St Futures Dip
items.story_title: Big Tech results and the AI spending boom
items.summary: Asian shares gave up early gains on Thursday after Google's owner Alphabet fell about 10% in late trading on heavy spending, pulling US share futures lower. The dollar held steady and oil slipped on a report that Washington is trying to restart talks with Iran.

beats.was: Stock markets have leaned on hopes for artificial-intelligence profits all year, and a slump in AI shares last week sent investors briefly into safe places such as the yen and the Swiss franc. Alphabet and Microsoft reported results after the US close on Wednesday, the same day the Federal Reserve held rates.
beats.happened: Alphabet's shares dropped about 10% after hours, wiping close to $400 billion off its value, while Microsoft rose about 3% on stronger cash flow. US tech futures fell about 1%, a broad index of Asian shares outside Japan fell 0.7% and South Korea's main index fell 2.6%. The dollar was flat after a small dip on Wednesday, and Brent crude eased 0.4% to about $115.
beats.means: Investors are again asking whether the huge sums poured into AI will pay off, which takes some of the shine off shares. So far it is a wobble, not a rush for safety: currency moves are small.
beats.fx: Weaker tech shares → a little less appetite for risk → mild help for the yen and franc, mild drag on the Australian dollar; if the selling deepens on Wall Street, that shelter demand grows.

impact.why: A tech-led share slide tends to send some money to the yen, but moves so far are small.
Usually tracks global shares, so a weaker tech mood weighs a little.
Another place investors park money when shares fall.

items.watch: How Wall Street opens on Thursday. A deeper tech slide would lift the yen and franc; a quick recovery would leave currencies to the US inflation figures and the European Central Bank.

items.headline: Gold slips after Fed holds rates, PCE inflation data in focus
items.story_title: Gold vs a hawkish Fed
items.summary: Gold eased to about $4,050 an ounce in Asian trading after the US Federal Reserve held rates but left a December hike likely. It is down about 2.5% in October, on course for a second monthly fall.

beats.was: Gold pays no interest, so it tends to suffer when US rates are expected to rise. The Fed raised rates in September and markets expect another hike in December because high energy prices are keeping inflation up. A slump in AI shares last week pushed gold to its lowest since July.
beats.happened: The Fed kept rates on hold on Wednesday in a 10-2 vote, the two dissenters wanting a hike. Spot gold slipped 0.4% to about $4,052 early Thursday in Asia. Goldman Sachs estimates central banks bought 79 tonnes of gold in August, a quarter of it by China.
beats.means: The pull of higher US rates is still beating gold's appeal as a shelter. Steady central-bank buying gives it a floor but has not been enough to turn the trend.
beats.fx: December hike still likely → holding gold costs more → gold under pressure; hot US inflation figures on Thursday → more pressure; soft figures → relief.

impact.why: A likely December US hike keeps weighing on a metal that pays no interest.

items.watch: Thursday's US September PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. A soft reading would ease hike bets and help gold.

items.headline: Oil falls as diplomacy hopes outweigh Middle East escalation fears
items.story_title: US-Iran war: talks vs new strikes
items.summary: Brent crude fell about 1% to near $114 a barrel on Thursday morning in London as fresh peace efforts between the US and Iran took some heat out of prices. Attacks on Saudi Arabia and on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz kept the drop small.

beats.was: Oil has been above $100 for weeks because the war between the US, Israel and Iran has largely shut the Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane for about a fifth of the world's oil. Yemen's Houthi rebels, who back Iran, said on Tuesday they hit Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery.
beats.happened: Brent slipped $1.27 to about $114 and US crude fell 1.5% to about $101 by mid-morning in London. The Wall Street Journal reported that Vice President JD Vance wrote to a senior Iranian security official to restart talks, and Qatar has put a new draft deal to Iran. But a Saudi-led coalition said it shot down a missile fired at eastern Saudi Arabia early Thursday, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers hit sea mines south of Hormuz.
beats.means: Talk of a deal is enough to shave a little off the war premium, but every new attack shows supply is still at risk. Worry that the US could strike Iran after its November 3 midterm elections keeps buyers from leaving.
beats.fx: Talks gain ground → oil eases → small relief for oil importers like the euro and yen, less help for the Canadian dollar; new attacks or US strikes → oil jumps back.

impact.why: Peace efforts trim the war premium, though attacks limit the fall.
Slightly lower oil means a little less support for a big Canadian export.
Japan imports nearly all its fuel, so cheaper oil eases pressure on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers Qatar's draft or the Vance letter, and any new Houthi strike on Saudi oil sites or tanker attacks near Hormuz.

items.headline: JD Vance sends letter to Iran hard-liner in bid to revive peace talks as Trump threatens strikes: Report
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: The Wall Street Journal reported that US Vice President JD Vance wrote to a senior Iranian security official to explore restarting peace talks. President Donald Trump denied ordering talks, saying the contact was about medical supplies.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war this year, and Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, largely shut. Trump has said there are no talks and has threatened new strikes, possibly soon after the November 3 US elections.
beats.happened: According to the Journal, Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a former Revolutionary Guards commander, asking whether a framework for talks could be set up. Trump said he had not told Vance to start talks and that Iran needed help with medical supplies; one source told the paper the letter went with Trump's knowledge.
beats.means: There is a back channel, but the White House is not owning it, and the threat of strikes is still on the table. That leaves the oil market caught between a small chance of a deal and a real chance of more fighting.
beats.fx: A live channel to Tehran → slightly lower odds of new strikes → oil eases a little; Trump's denial and strike threats → the risk premium in oil stays → support for the Canadian dollar, pressure on the yen and euro as oil importers.

impact.why: Hints of talks pull oil down a touch, but the denial and strike threats keep the war premium.
Shelter demand fades on talk of talks and returns if strikes look closer.
Same push and pull on demand for safety.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the letter or either side confirms contact. A public reply would pull oil lower; new US strikes would send it and shelter assets sharply higher.

items.headline: US Market Wrap: Stocks gain as tech climbs while Dollar takes a hit post Fed
items.story_title: Federal Reserve: the October 28 decision
items.summary: The dollar gave back part of its recent gains after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press briefing on Wednesday, as he made no promise of a December hike. Short-term US yields dipped while long-term yields rose, and US shares closed a little higher.

beats.was: The dollar had climbed to a two-week high going into the US Federal Reserve's decision, on bets that the Fed would sound ready to raise rates again in December. The Fed raised rates in September, the first time in three years, because the Iran war pushed US inflation up.
beats.happened: The Fed kept rates at 3.75% to 4%, with two officials voting for a hike. After Warsh's briefing the dollar index slipped to about 102.1 from about 102.5 earlier in the day. Market odds of a December hike eased to about 85% from about 90%. The two-year Treasury yield fell slightly, the 10-year rose to about 5.05%, and oil closed higher on US-Iran tensions.
beats.means: Markets heard a Fed that wants more data before acting again, so the push behind the dollar faded a little. Long-term yields rising while short-term ones dipped suggests some worry that the Fed is moving too slowly against inflation.
beats.fx: No firm December promise → hike odds a touch lower → the dollar loses some of its pre-meeting gains; a December hike is still the base case → the dollar keeps most of its rate support.

impact.why: Gave back some of its run-up as Warsh kept December open; hike odds slipped only slightly.
Gained on a softer US dollar and higher Canadian yields after the Bank of Canada's hike.
Edged up against a softer dollar ahead of Thursday's European Central Bank decision.

items.watch: Thursday's US figures: third-quarter growth and the September PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. Hot numbers would firm up a December hike and help the dollar back.

items.headline: Fed holds rates in a split vote; Warsh keeps December open and changes the meeting calendar
items.story_title: Federal Reserve: the October 28 decision
items.summary: The US Federal Reserve kept its rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday, as expected, with two officials voting for a hike. At his press briefing, Chair Kevin Warsh made no promise on December and said that from 2027 one meeting a year will skip the rate vote.

beats.was: The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years, because the Iran war pushed fuel prices up and US inflation reached 3.7% in September. Markets saw a pause this time as near certain and were already pricing a likely hike at the December 8-9 meeting.
beats.happened: The vote was 10-2: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted a quarter-point hike. The statement called growth strong and said more information will help the Fed set the right level of rates. At the briefing, Chair Kevin Warsh repeated that line and announced that from 2027 one of the eight yearly meetings will be a strategy session with no rate vote and no statement, rising to two in 2028.
beats.means: December is not settled: the Fed wants to see more data first, but two votes for a hike show pressure inside the bank. Markets still see about an 86% chance of a December hike, up from 78% on Tuesday. Fewer voting meetings from 2027 mean fewer dates on which rates can change.
beats.fx: Pause with hawkish votes, no promise on December → hike odds stay high but depend on the data → the dollar keeps its rate support and stays near its high for the year, waiting on Thursday's figures.

impact.why: Expected pause; hike votes and high December odds support it, while Warsh's wait-for-data tone holds it back.
No hike today helps gold a little; a likely December hike still weighs on it.

items.watch: Thursday's US figures: third-quarter growth and the September PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge; a hot reading firms up December.

items.headline: British markets take Healey's first budget in their stride
items.story_title: UK budget: Chancellor Healey's first, on October 28
items.summary: UK government borrowing costs fell after Chancellor John Healey's first budget, and shares rose. The pound slipped to about $1.33, moved more by the strong dollar than by the budget.

beats.was: Britain's bond market has been touchy since the 2022 mini-budget, when unfunded tax cuts sent borrowing costs and the pound sharply lower. Investors feared Healey would leave too little spare room under the government's borrowing rules.
beats.happened: Healey left £15 billion of room, close to what economists expected but below the £23.6 billion set in March. The yield on 10-year UK government bonds fell to about 5.31% and on 30-year bonds to about 5.70%. Big banks' shares rose more than 3% after a smaller-than-feared rise in their extra tax.
beats.means: The budget passed without a scare, which removes one worry for the pound. Attention moves back to the Bank of England, which decides on November 5.
beats.fx: A calm budget → no extra risk premium on UK debt → the pound trades on the dollar and the Bank of England, not on fiscal fear.

impact.why: Budget fear has passed, but the pound still slipped against a firm dollar.

items.watch: The Bank of England decision on Thursday, November 5.

items.headline: US crude and distillate inventories fall, gasoline stocks rise, EIA says
items.story_title: Iran war: the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: US crude stocks fell by 1.9 million barrels last week when no change was expected, as exports jumped, while gasoline stocks rose by 3.9 million barrels instead of falling. Brent rose to about $115.70.

beats.was: With Gulf supply cut by the Iran war, buyers abroad have leaned on US oil, and the weekly report from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows how fast US stocks are being drawn down.
beats.happened: For the week to October 23, US crude stocks fell to 410.6 million barrels as exports rose by 1.4 million barrels a day, and stocks on the Gulf Coast hit their lowest since December 2024. Gasoline stocks rose because Americans bought less of it, while diesel and heating oil stocks fell. One shipping tracker said the export jump may be overstated.
beats.means: Crude keeps leaving the US quickly, which shows how tight world supply is. Weaker US gasoline buying is the one soft spot.
beats.fx: Falling US crude stocks → a tighter oil market → support for oil, and through oil for the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: Crude stocks fell when no change was expected, though gasoline rose.
Firm oil helps Canada's biggest export.

items.watch: Next week's EIA report on November 4, and whether US exports stay this high.

items.headline: Iran calls Qatar's latest peace proposals 'unacceptable' as US strike fears grow
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Qatar's mediators brought a list of ideas Iran cannot accept, not a real offer, and that Iran will not give ground on its nuclear programme. Other reports say Tehran is still weighing a Qatari draft.

beats.was: The US-Iran war, which began in February, has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane for much of the Gulf's oil, largely shut, with a US blockade of Iranian ports. Qatar and Pakistan are leading efforts to end it, and Qatar handed Iran a seven-day step-by-step plan on Sunday.
beats.happened: On Wednesday a senior Iranian official dismissed Qatar's suggestions and said Iran would not let its enriched nuclear material leave the country. The two sides disagree on order: Washington wants the nuclear programme on the table first, while Tehran wants the US blockade and oil sanctions lifted first.
beats.means: The messages from Tehran are mixed on the same day, so the peace path looks shakier than it did this morning. With reports that the US is preparing strikes after the November 3 US elections, the risk of a longer war has not faded.
beats.fx: Weaker hopes for a deal → Gulf oil stays at risk → support for oil prices and for gold as shelter.

impact.why: Cools hopes that a deal will reopen Gulf supply soon.
Keeps war risk, and demand for shelter, alive.

items.watch: Iran's formal reply to Qatar, expected by the end of the week, and any US decision on new strikes.

items.headline: Iran 'welcomes negotiations' after reported Qatari-mediated draft deal
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: An Iranian official said Tehran is open to talks after Qatar's mediators handed it a draft deal to end the war with the US. Iran is expected to answer by the end of the week.

beats.was: The US-Iran war has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane for much of the Gulf's oil, under a US blockade of Iranian ships since July. A Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish delegation met Iranian leaders in Tehran on Monday with no clear result.
beats.happened: Qatar's draft, handed over on Sunday, sets out seven days of step-by-step goodwill moves by both sides, backed by several guarantor countries, possibly starting early next week. Iran, for its part, asked the visitors to win US support for a two-week pause in fighting across the region, after which talks would restart and Hormuz would slowly reopen.
beats.means: Both sides now have a written plan on the table, which is the first concrete path to an end of the war in weeks. Nothing is agreed yet, and Iran says it cannot rein in Yemen's Houthi rebels, who keep hitting Saudi targets.
beats.fx: A real chance of talks → less fear for Gulf oil supply → mild pressure on oil prices and on demand for gold as shelter.

impact.why: A draft peace plan eases supply fears a little, but nothing is signed.
Talk of a pause trims demand for shelter.

items.watch: Iran's reply to the Qatari draft by the end of the week, and whether the US backs a two-week pause.

items.headline: Bank of Canada raises key interest rate, says another hike possible
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: the October 28 decision
items.summary: The Bank of Canada raised its rate from 2.25% to 2.5% on Wednesday, its first hike since 2023, and said it may need to go higher. It now sees inflation staying near 3% through most of next year.

beats.was: Canadian inflation reached 3.2% in September, above the bank's 1% to 3% target range, mostly because of energy and transport costs tied to the Iran war. Markets had mostly priced a quarter-point rise.
beats.happened: The bank lifted its rate a quarter point to 2.5%, still below the level it sees as neutral. Governor Tiff Macklem said a further rise may be needed and the bank will move carefully. It raised its 2027 inflation forecast to 3.1% from 2.0% and expects inflation back near 2% only by mid-2028; it also lifted its growth forecasts, while warning new US tariffs will slow the last quarter of this year.
beats.means: The hike itself was expected. The new part is the open door to more and a much higher inflation path, which tells markets the bank worries that high fuel costs are spreading to other prices.
beats.fx: Hike plus a hint of more → Canadian rates stay attractive for longer → some support for the loonie.

impact.why: Expected hike, but the open door to more adds a little support.

items.watch: How the loonie trades once the Fed decides at 1:00 PM CT, and Canada's October inflation figure in November.

items.headline: UK Budget Shrinks Fiscal Buffer Without Market Shock; Fed Dissent in Focus
items.story_title: UK budget: Chancellor Healey's first, on October 28
items.summary: Chancellor John Healey's first budget cut the government's spare room under its borrowing rules to £15 billion, from about £24 billion in March. The pound and UK government bonds barely moved.

beats.was: Investors had worried that a weak budget could push UK long-term borrowing costs, already near their highest in decades, even higher. The pound had slipped to its lowest in about two weeks going in.
beats.happened: Healey said the government will have £15 billion of room under its rules by 2029–30, down from £23.6 billion in March, as the Iran war weighs on the economy. The 10-year UK government bond yield edged down to about 5.34% from 5.36% before the speech, and the pound held near $1.329 and flat against the euro.
beats.means: There was no fresh scare, so the pound avoids a hit for now. But the buffer is smaller, so any future miss on growth or borrowing would leave less room before taxes or spending have to change.
beats.fx: Smaller buffer but no bond-market alarm → no new pressure on the pound today → focus moves to the Bank of England on November 5.

impact.why: A thinner buffer, but bonds and the pound shrugged it off.

items.watch: Whether UK long-term borrowing costs stay calm into the Bank of England decision on November 5.

items.headline: US Goods Trade Deficit Widens to $134.9B as Capital Goods Imports Surge
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: The US gap between goods imported and exported grew to $134.9 billion in September, wider than forecast, as companies bought more machinery and equipment abroad. The dollar did not react.

beats.was: This early monthly trade figure feeds into estimates of US growth for the July–September quarter, which comes out later this week.
beats.happened: The goods deficit widened by $2.8 billion to $134.9 billion, against forecasts near $129 billion. Imports rose 2.4%, led by a 7.5% jump in equipment and machinery, while exports rose 2.6%. Stockpiles held by wholesalers rose a bit more than expected.
beats.means: More imports subtract a little from measured US growth for the quarter, but buying equipment also points to firms still investing. It does little to change the view that the Fed holds today and leans toward a December hike.
beats.fx: Wider trade gap → slightly weaker growth math → a small drag on the dollar that the Fed decision will likely swamp.

impact.why: Bigger-than-expected gap trims growth estimates a little.

items.watch: The first estimate of US growth for July–September on Thursday, October 29.

items.headline: US Tells Ships to Avoid Unnecessary Transits Through Hormuz
items.story_title: Iran war: the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: The US Navy told ships on Wednesday to stay clear of the Strait of Hormuz unless they must pass, and warned of searches tied to its blockade of Iran. It gave no reason for the new notice.

beats.was: The US has blocked Iranian shipping through the Strait of Hormuz since mid-July. Even so, tankers willing to take the risk have pushed Gulf oil flows back near prewar levels, while Iran's own exports are close to zero and its attacks on ships hit almost 30 in October.
beats.happened: US Naval Forces Central Command, which runs the blockade, advised vessels with no need to cross the Gulf of Oman and Hormuz to keep well away, and told those that must cross to expect delays. Even neutral ships with neutral cargo may be questioned, boarded and searched.
beats.means: The last notice like this came when the blockade began, so a fresh one hints that the US is tightening enforcement. It lands a day after a report that the US told Gulf states to prepare for possible strikes on Iran after the November 3 US elections.
beats.fx: Slower or riskier passage through Hormuz → higher shipping and insurance costs → some support for oil prices.

impact.why: Tighter checks could slow tanker traffic, though no oil has been lost yet.

items.watch: Whether tanker traffic through Hormuz slows in the coming days, and any US explanation for the notice.

items.headline: European Central Bank Expected to Hold Interest Rates at 2.5%
items.story_title: ECB: the October 29 decision
items.summary: The European Central Bank is expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, October 29, after two hikes this year. Markets still see more rises over the next year, with one in December the most common forecast.

beats.was: The ECB raised rates in June and September as war-driven energy costs pushed euro-area inflation to 3.8% in September, from 2.1% in February. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, is 2.5%.
beats.happened: Money markets expect no change this week but two to three more hikes over the next 12 months; a Bloomberg survey of economists sees one last rise to 2.75% in December. Chief Economist Philip Lane and President Christine Lagarde have both warned that the sharp rise in long-term borrowing costs is already slowing the economy.
beats.means: A pause is priced in, so what matters is the tone. If the bank sounds worried about high bond yields and France's budget strain, markets may cut back their bets on more hikes.
beats.fx: Hold expected → little reaction on its own; a softer tone on future hikes would weigh on the euro, a firm one would help it.

impact.why: A hold is expected; the euro moves on the hint about December.

items.watch: Lagarde's press conference on Thursday, October 29, and whether she keeps a December hike open.

items.headline: US warns Persian Gulf states of possible post-election Iran strikes - WSJ
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: The US has reportedly told Gulf Arab governments to get ready for a short, heavy US attack on Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections. The White House would not comment, and the Wall Street Journal says no final decision has been made.

beats.was: The US and Israel fought a war with Iran this year that partly blocked the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. Talks with Iran, helped by Qatar, have stalled in recent days.
beats.happened: The Wall Street Journal reported that the US warned several Gulf states, through diplomats and the military, to prepare for a possible short, intense campaign against Iran after the midterms. President Trump is said to lean toward a large strike on Iran's infrastructure and nuclear sites. The US is moving air-defence systems, fresh munitions, bombers and another aircraft carrier group into the region.
beats.means: This puts a rough date on the risk of the war restarting: the days after November 3. Until then, the chance of new fighting keeps a fear premium in oil and keeps demand for safe places to hold money.
beats.fx: Talk of new US strikes → bigger risk to Gulf oil → higher oil, which helps Canada and hurts Japan and Europe, and more demand for the dollar and Swiss franc as shelter.

impact.why: Puts a possible date on new fighting near the Gulf's oil routes.
War fears add to demand for the dollar as shelter.
The franc draws money when war risk rises.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so the fuel bill risk rises.

items.watch: Whether talks with Iran restart before November 3, or the White House confirms or denies the plan.

items.headline: Asian stocks rally, $US steady before Fed decision
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: Asian shares jumped on Wednesday on renewed excitement about AI companies, with South Korea's main index up more than 3%. The dollar held near a two-week high before the US Federal Reserve's decision.

beats.was: The US-Israeli war with Iran has kept oil high and inflation worries alive, and markets expect the Fed to hold rates on Wednesday while debating a December hike.
beats.happened: Japan's Nikkei rose 1.2% and Korea's KOSPI more than 3%, led by chipmaker SK Hynix's much bigger profit and new funding plans from large tech firms. The dollar index sat near 102.4. Brent oil edged up to about $114 a barrel and gold was flat near $4,058.
beats.means: Investors are confident enough to buy shares, which cuts demand for safe places to park money. The dollar is holding firm mainly because a hawkish Fed message is still possible.
beats.fx: Rising shares → less need for shelter → yen and Swiss franc lose some support; the Fed decision still sets the dollar's next move.

impact.why: Rising shares cut demand for the yen as shelter.
Holds near a two-week high before the Fed.
Less demand for shelter when shares rally.

items.watch: The Fed decision at 1:00 PM CT and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference at 1:30 PM CT.

items.headline: AUD/NZD in focus as hawkish RBA signals clash with RBNZ's surprise 4-3 hold
items.story_title: RBA: a fifth hike on November 3?
items.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock told senators inflation will likely run above the bank's August forecast. On the same morning New Zealand's central bank skipped an expected hike, pulling the two currencies apart.

beats.was: Australia's central bank has raised its rate four times this year, by a full percentage point in total, to 4.60%. It meets again on November 2-3.
beats.happened: Speaking to a Senate committee hours after hot Australian inflation figures, Bullock said higher energy costs and a slightly tighter job market mean inflation is likely to beat the August forecast. She said the board's key question next week is whether the hikes so far are enough. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand, meanwhile, held its rate when a rise was expected.
beats.means: One central bank is still leaning toward more hikes while its neighbour just paused. That gap is why the Australian dollar climbed to its strongest against the kiwi in over a decade.
beats.fx: Australian bank open to a fifth hike, New Zealand bank waiting → wider rate gap between the two → Australian dollar stronger against the kiwi.

impact.why: The governor's warning on inflation keeps a November hike on the table.
Loses ground against the Australian dollar as the two rate paths split.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of Australia's decision on Tuesday, November 3; a hold there would narrow the gap again.

items.headline: RBNZ Surprises with 4–3 Hold at 2.75%, but Further Rate Hikes Remain Likely
items.story_title: RBNZ: the October 28 decision
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand kept its rate at 2.75% when almost everyone expected a rise to 3%. The kiwi fell about 1.7% to roughly 55.9 US cents.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand raised its rate in July and September to fight inflation pushed up by fuel costs from the Iran war. Markets saw about a 90% chance of a third rise on Wednesday, October 28, and all five big New Zealand banks forecast one.
beats.happened: The bank held at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote. Governor Anna Breman and three others wanted to wait and see how the earlier hikes are working; three members wanted a rise now. All seven agreed more tightening is likely, but the timing depends on the data. Inflation slowed to 3.7% in the third quarter, below the bank's forecast.
beats.means: Markets had treated the hike as done, so the hold forced a quick rethink. The bank still sounds ready to raise rates later, so this reads more as a delay than a turn toward cuts.
beats.fx: Expected hike didn't come → lower New Zealand rates for longer than priced → less reason to hold the kiwi → New Zealand dollar weaker, especially against the Australian dollar.

impact.why: A hike nearly everyone expected didn't happen, so rate expectations dropped fast.
Gains against the kiwi as the two central banks move apart.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's December decision, which comes with new forecasts. A weaker kiwi raises import prices, which could bring the hike back sooner.

items.headline: CPI rose 4.3% in the year to September 2026
items.story_title: RBA: a fifth hike on November 3?
items.summary: Australian prices rose 4.3% in the year to September, up from 4.0% and a little above the 4.2% forecasters expected. The core measure the Reserve Bank of Australia watches rose 1.0% in the quarter, above the bank's own forecast.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised its rate four times this year, to 4.60%, as higher fuel costs from the Iran war push up prices. It decides again on November 3, and markets already leaned toward a fifth hike.
beats.happened: The Australian Bureau of Statistics said prices rose 0.8% in September alone and 1.3% over the July-to-September quarter. Petrol was up 9.4% in the month after a 14.8% jump in August. The trimmed mean, which drops the biggest price swings, held at 3.6% a year and rose 1.0% in the quarter, against the bank's August forecast of 0.8%. Housing and electricity were the largest drivers.
beats.means: Inflation is running faster than the central bank planned for, and not only because of fuel: the core measure is also too high. That makes a hike on November 3 harder to skip.
beats.fx: Inflation above the bank's forecast → November hike more likely → wider rate gap with other countries → support for the Australian dollar.

impact.why: Core inflation beat the central bank's forecast, firming up a November hike.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of Australia's decision on Tuesday, November 3.

items.headline: Exit polls suggest a rebuke of Netanyahu but no clear winner in Israel's election
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Israel's election on Tuesday produced no clear winner. Exit polls put Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot roughly level, both far from a majority.

beats.was: Israel and the US have been at war with Iran, which has disrupted oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Some investors saw a Netanyahu loss as a way to lower the risk of the war widening.
beats.happened: Television exit polls gave each side about 51 of the 120 seats in parliament, with Arab parties holding about 18. Neither camp has a clear path to the 61 seats needed to govern. Israel's president will ask the leader with the best chance to try to form a coalition; if no one can, another election could come early next year.
beats.means: There is no quick answer on who leads Israel through the Iran war, so the vote does not change the war risk built into oil prices for now. Exit polls can be wrong, and final counts could still shift the picture.
beats.fx: Deadlock → Iran war risk stays as it was → oil stays high; little change for the dollar or oil-linked currencies.

impact.why: No winner yet, so the vote neither raises nor lowers war risk.

items.watch: Final vote counts and whom Israel's president asks to form a government.

items.headline: Canadian Dollar and Business Outlook: Loonie down after BoC raises key interest rate
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: the October 28 decision
items.summary: The Canadian dollar edged down to about 1.406 per US dollar after the Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5%. The hike had been expected, so it gave the currency little lift.

beats.was: The Bank of Canada had held its rate at 2.25% for a year. Higher oil and fuel prices from the Iran war have pushed Canadian inflation up, and economists widely expected a quarter-point rise.
beats.happened: The bank raised its rate to 2.5% on Wednesday, its first hike in three years, and said more rises are possible. The Canadian dollar slipped to about 71.1 US cents from 71.2 on Tuesday, while the US dollar stayed strong before the Federal Reserve decision.
beats.means: Markets had already priced the hike, so the news added little. The bank's hint of more rises keeps a floor under the currency, but the US dollar's strength matters more for now.
beats.fx: An expected hike → little new support → the Canadian dollar follows the US dollar and oil.

impact.why: The hike was priced in; a hint of more gives only mild support.

items.watch: The Fed decision at 1:00 PM CT today, and Canada's jobs report on Friday, November 6.

items.headline: Gold Retreats Ahead of Fed Decision as Dollar Strengthens
items.story_title: Gold vs a hawkish Fed
items.summary: Gold slipped back below $4,050 on Wednesday, ending a two-day bounce, as the dollar held near a two-week high before the Fed decision.

beats.was: Gold fell about 4% last week and hit a three-month low early this week as markets came to expect a US rate hike in December.
beats.happened: Gold dipped below $4,050 in European trading. Markets still see over an 80% chance of a December Fed hike, and high energy prices keep inflation worries alive. Claims of a Houthi missile hit on Saudi Arabia and reports of possible US strikes on Iran lifted demand for the dollar rather than for gold.
beats.means: Higher US rates make a metal that pays no interest less appealing, and for now the dollar is the shelter of choice when Middle East risks flare.
beats.fx: Hike bets and a firm dollar → gold loses its bounce → $4,000 is the line markets watch.

impact.why: December hike bets and a firm dollar cap the rebound.
The dollar is drawing the shelter demand.

items.watch: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's tone on a December hike after the 1:00 PM CT decision.

items.headline: Oil up over 1% as Saudi Arabian refinery attack reignites supply risk concerns
items.story_title: Saudi Arabia: Houthi attacks on oil and airports
items.summary: Oil rose more than 1% on Wednesday, with Brent near $115, after Yemen's Houthi rebels said they hit Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery. Saudi Arabia had not confirmed the strike, and a US industry report showed crude stocks falling.

beats.was: The Houthis, an Iran-aligned group in Yemen, have stepped up missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia during the Iran war. Oil had slipped nearly $2 on Tuesday on hopes for peace talks in Tehran.
beats.happened: Brent rose about $1.40 to roughly $115 a barrel by Wednesday morning in London, and US crude rose about 1.6% to $101.50. The Houthis said a missile hit Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, which processes 550,000 barrels a day; Saudi Arabia had not confirmed it. The American Petroleum Institute, a US industry group, reported a 2 million barrel fall in US crude stocks when a small rise was expected. ING said markets see a higher chance of the fighting flaring up again.
beats.means: Oil won back most of Tuesday's drop. No lost supply has been shown, so this is fear being priced back in rather than a real shortage.
beats.fx: Attack claims on Saudi oil → oil back up → helps oil sellers like Canada, hurts oil buyers like Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Unconfirmed refinery hit plus falling US stocks win back Tuesday's drop.
Higher oil lifts what Canada earns from exports.
Dearer crude raises Japan's import bill.

items.watch: Official US stock figures at 9:30 AM CT and any Saudi word on damage to the refinery.

items.headline: Sterling Slips Ahead of UK Budget Amid Bond Market Worries
items.story_title: UK budget: Chancellor Healey's first, on October 28
items.summary: The pound eased to about $1.329 before Chancellor John Healey's first budget, due at 7:30 AM CT on Wednesday. His room to spend is thin, and one strategist warned that a market-friendly budget is already expected, so the easier way for the pound is down.

beats.was: Britain's long-term borrowing costs hit their highest since 1998 earlier this month. Healey, the finance minister, took over from Rachel Reeves, who had already raised taxes heavily.
beats.happened: The pound slipped 0.1% to about $1.329 and 83.7 pence per euro on Wednesday morning. Official forecasters put the government's spare room under its own borrowing rules at only about £15 billion. Higher taxes on banks, betting firms and online marketplaces are expected, with little new borrowing. Markets still expect the Bank of England to raise rates on November 5.
beats.means: Investors expect a careful budget. If Healey borrows more than planned, bond and pound sellers have room to push; a careful budget mostly leaves things as they are.
beats.fx: Thin room to spend → any extra borrowing would hit UK bonds → the pound is more exposed to a bad surprise than a good one.

impact.why: Slips before a budget where a borrowing surprise is the main risk.

items.watch: How much new borrowing Healey announces at 7:30 AM CT, and how UK 10- and 30-year bond yields react.

items.headline: USD/CAD Extends Rally Ahead of BoC and Fed Decisions
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: the October 28 decision
items.summary: The Canadian dollar weakened for a second day, to just over 1.40 per US dollar, before the Bank of Canada's decision at 8:45 AM CT and the US Federal Reserve's at 1:00 PM CT. A firm US dollar outweighed a rebound in oil.

beats.was: The Bank of Canada has kept its main rate at 2.25% for a year, but war-driven fuel prices pushed Canadian inflation to 3.1% in September. Most economists expect a quarter-point rise on Wednesday.
beats.happened: The US dollar rose to a one-week high against the loonie in Asian trading, moving above 1.40 after a low near 1.397 last week. The US dollar has gained for four straight days on bets the Fed will raise rates in December. Oil climbed again after two days of losses, which limited the loonie's fall.
beats.means: A Bank of Canada hike is mostly expected, so it would only steady the loonie. A surprise hold would hurt it more, as New Zealand's surprise hold hurt the kiwi earlier on Wednesday.
beats.fx: Bank of Canada hike expected → a hike steadies the loonie, a hold would knock it lower; the Fed's tone later decides the US dollar side.

impact.why: Slips for a second day before its own rate decision.
Four days of gains on bets for a December Fed hike.

items.watch: The Bank of Canada's decision and forecasts at 8:45 AM CT; a hold would surprise.

items.headline: Dollar steady ahead of Fed decision, kiwi slumps after RBNZ holds
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: The dollar held at its highest since mid-October before Wednesday's Federal Reserve decision, where a hold is about 91% priced. The euro and pound were flat near $1.113 and $1.331.

beats.was: US inflation is running near 3.7%, partly from war-driven oil prices, and strong US data this week pushed the dollar up for three days.
beats.happened: The dollar index stayed near 102.4 after a 0.3% gain on Tuesday. Futures put about a 91% chance on the Fed holding rates on Wednesday. The yen was little changed near 157.8 per dollar, and the US 10-year yield sat just under 5%.
beats.means: A hold is expected, so the decision itself should not move much. What matters is whether Fed Chair Kevin Warsh backs the December hike markets are leaning toward.
beats.fx: Hold expected → focus on Warsh's tone → backing a December hike would lift the dollar, doubts about it would pull it back.

impact.why: Holds a two-week high as markets lean toward a December hike.
Stuck near two-week lows against a firm dollar.

items.watch: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's comments on a December hike after the 1:00 PM CT decision.

items.headline: EUR/JPY Drops as Intervention Jitters and BoJ Lift Yen
items.story_title: Japan: official warnings over a weak yen
items.summary: The yen firmed against the euro on Wednesday, to about 175.65 yen per euro, after Japan's finance minister warned again that Tokyo is ready to act in the currency market. The Bank of Japan meets on Friday.

beats.was: The yen has been weak, near 158 per US dollar, because Japan's interest rates are far below those in the US and Europe. Japan's government has bought yen in the past to slow sharp falls.
beats.happened: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Tuesday that the government is ready to take decisive action in the currency market if needed. The euro then slipped against the yen in early European trading. Analysts at MUFG, a big Japanese bank, see buying as not imminent and point to 160 yen per dollar as the likely trigger.
beats.means: The warnings make yen sellers more careful, so the yen's fall slows. The Bank of Japan is expected to hold its rate at 1.25% on Friday, October 30, while markets see about an 80% chance of a hike in December, which also gives the yen some support.
beats.fx: Firmer warnings + a likely December hike in Japan → less room for the yen to keep falling → the yen steadies against the euro and dollar; no action yet → the rate gap still weighs on it.

impact.why: Official warnings and December hike hopes give the yen a floor.
Slipped against the yen ahead of Thursday's European Central Bank decision, expected to be a hold.

items.watch: Friday's Bank of Japan decision and any hint on December, or a fast slide in the yen toward 160 per dollar.

items.headline: ECB to hold rates as investors focus on French bonds, Lagarde's future
items.story_title: ECB: the October 29 decision
items.summary: The European Central Bank is expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, with markets pricing about three more hikes ahead. Investors care more about France's borrowing costs and whether President Christine Lagarde leaves early.

beats.was: The ECB raised rates in June and September as the oil shock from the Iran war lifted euro-area inflation to a three-year high. France's budget troubles have pushed its borrowing costs to some of the highest in 25 years, well above Germany's.
beats.happened: Reuters expects a hold at 2.5%, with markets betting on roughly three more quarter-point rises, to 3.25%, and a December move still seen as likely. Help for French bonds looks unlikely for now. Lagarde's term runs for another year, but she may leave before France's spring presidential election; Dutch and Spanish former central bank chiefs Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernández de Cos are named as possible successors.
beats.means: A hold is expected, so the euro's reaction depends on tone: whether the bank keeps December open, and whether it sounds worried about France. Uncertainty over the next president adds a little extra doubt.
beats.fx: Clear signal that more hikes are coming → euro support; a softer tone or worry about French debt → euro weaker. A Lagarde exit story → mild uncertainty for the euro.

impact.why: A hold is priced; the euro's move hinges on the December signal and the bank's view of France.

items.watch: The decision at 8:15 AM CT Thursday and the press briefing 30 minutes later: any firm hint of a December hike, or any mention of help for bond markets.

items.headline: Gold Price Today: Can $4,000 Hold as December Fed Hike Bets Hit 82%?
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: Gold dipped to $4,000 and bounced to about $4,024 on Tuesday as the dollar hit a near two-week high. Markets now see about an 82% chance the US Federal Reserve raises rates in December.

beats.was: Gold fell about 4% last week from record highs as the Fed, fighting inflation of 3.7%, signalled more rate rises. The Fed decides on Wednesday, October 28, and the PCE inflation measure, the one the Fed watches most, comes out on Thursday.
beats.happened: Gold touched $4,000 early Tuesday, down 0.4%, then recovered to around $4,024 by midday in London. Futures pricing compiled by CME shows about an 82% chance of a December hike, up from about 73% last week. Gold is still below its average of the past 20 days.
beats.means: Buyers keep stepping in at $4,000, but rising odds of higher US rates make a metal that pays no interest less attractive. A firm Fed or hot inflation figures this week would add to the pressure.
beats.fx: Higher odds of a US hike → a stronger dollar → gold costs more for foreign buyers and struggles to rise.

impact.why: Rising hike odds weigh on gold, though $4,000 keeps attracting buyers.
Markets lean more toward a December hike, which supports the dollar.

items.watch: Whether gold holds $4,000 after Wednesday's Fed decision and Thursday's PCE inflation report.

items.headline: What to expect from the Fed as Warsh weighs hot inflation, oil and US midterms
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: The US Federal Reserve is almost certain to leave rates alone on Wednesday, but inflation near 3.7% keeps a December hike likely. The open questions are what Chair Kevin Warsh hints at and how many officials vote for a hike now.

beats.was: The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, as war-driven fuel costs pushed US inflation back up. It meets again on Wednesday, October 28, six days before the US midterm elections.
beats.happened: A Euronews preview says markets see better than a 90% chance of no change on Wednesday and about a 73% chance of a quarter-point hike in December. Consumer prices rose 3.7% over the year to September, up from 3.4%, with petrol behind more than half of the rise. Two regional Fed presidents, Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Lorie Logan of Dallas, have said rates are not yet high enough, so some officials may vote against a hold.
beats.means: A hold is already expected, so the dollar will react to the tone: whether Warsh leaves December open and whether several officials push for a hike now. Political pressure from the White House before the vote is a reason he may stay vague.
beats.fx: Inflation still rising and possible votes for a hike → a firm-sounding Fed → support for the dollar; a vague message close to the election → that support fades.

impact.why: A preview: a December hike is mostly expected, so only a firmer tone would add support.
Talk of more US hikes weighs on a metal that pays no interest.

items.watch: How many Fed officials vote for a hike on Wednesday, and whether Warsh rules December in or out.

items.headline: Government issues debt at highest interest rate since financial crisis on eve of Budget
items.story_title: UK budget: Chancellor Healey's first, on October 28
items.summary: Britain sold about £4.5bn of five-year government bonds at a 5.04% yield, the most it has paid on that kind of debt since 2008. Demand was strong, but the cost shows how little room Chancellor John Healey has in Wednesday's budget.

beats.was: UK Chancellor John Healey presents his first budget on Wednesday, October 28. He has kept the rule that day-to-day spending must be covered by taxes by 2029, and UK borrowing costs are the highest in the G7 after the Iran war pushed up oil prices and inflation.
beats.happened: The Debt Management Office, which sells UK government debt, sold bonds due in 2032 at a yield of 5.04%, the highest for such a sale since the 2008 financial crisis. Buyers offered 3.5 times the amount on sale. Interest on the national debt now costs more than £115bn a year.
beats.means: Investors are still willing to lend to Britain, but only at a high price. That squeezes Healey's budget: any surprise jump in planned borrowing could push yields higher still.
beats.fx: Strong demand at the sale → no sign of a buyers' strike → the pound is steady; record borrowing costs → little room for budget surprises → the pound is exposed if the plan disappoints.

impact.why: Strong demand for UK debt, but at a cost that leaves the budget little room.

items.watch: Whether Healey's plan on Wednesday raises borrowing more than expected, and how UK bond yields react.

items.headline: US Consumer Confidence Increased in October
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: US consumer confidence jumped to 91.7 in October, far above the 81 economists expected, as people felt better about business conditions and petrol got cheaper. It is one more sign the US economy is holding up the day before the Fed decides.

beats.was: The US Federal Reserve decides on rates on Wednesday, October 28, and is expected to hold; markets mostly expect a hike in December. In September the Conference Board's consumer confidence index had sunk to its lowest level in years as war-driven fuel prices squeezed households.
beats.happened: The Conference Board, a private research group, said its index rose 7.5 points to 91.7 in October, from a September figure revised up to 84.2; economists polled by Reuters had expected about 81. Views of today's conditions and of the next six months both improved, helped by falling petrol prices. Households still expect prices to rise 5.8% over the next year and plan to spend a bit less on services and big purchases.
beats.means: Americans feel steadier than forecasters thought, which makes it easier for the Fed to keep talking about a December hike. High expected inflation and softer spending plans keep it from being a clean all-clear.
beats.fx: Confident consumers and high expected inflation → firmer case for a December Fed hike → support for the dollar; weaker spending plans → that support has a limit.

impact.why: A big beat on consumer mood backs the case for a December Fed hike.
Higher odds of a US hike weigh on a metal that pays no interest.

items.watch: What Fed Chair Kevin Warsh says about December on Wednesday, and Thursday's US inflation figure.

items.headline: Iran says oil tanker catches fire after hitting naval mine east of Strait of Hormuz
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran's navy says an oil tanker caught fire after hitting mines just east of the Strait of Hormuz, and repeated that ships may only pass with its permission. It gave no name, flag or crew details.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane between Iran and Oman, carries about a fifth of the world's oil. During the eight-month Iran war, Tehran has said ships need its approval to pass, and attacks on tankers there have pushed oil prices up.
beats.happened: On Tuesday Iran's navy said a tanker that had turned off its tracking signal hit naval mines in a restricted area east of the strait and caught fire. It said the strait stays closed and unsafe for any ship that does not coordinate with Iran's armed forces. The ship has not been identified, and the claim has not been confirmed by others.
beats.means: Iran is showing it can still make the route dangerous even while its neighbours hold peace talks. Iran has made similar mine claims before, and US forces have called some of them false, so traders treat each new one with caution.
beats.fx: Mines in the main oil route → more risk that oil supply is cut → a higher price floor for oil, a small help for Canada's loonie and a weight on big oil buyers like Japan.

impact.why: An unconfirmed mine strike adds to supply worries but echoes earlier claims.
Japan imports almost all its oil, so supply scares raise its fuel bill.

items.watch: Whether the tanker is identified and whether shipping firms pull back from the route.

items.headline: Precious metals weaken as Hormuz uncertainty keeps oil elevated ahead of Fed decision
items.story_title: Gold vs a hawkish Fed
items.summary: Gold dipped just under $4,000 an ounce on Tuesday morning and silver fell about 2%. High oil keeps US inflation worries alive, which supports the case for more Fed hikes and hurts metals that pay no interest.

beats.was: Gold fell about 4% last week. The US Federal Reserve is expected to hold rates on Wednesday, October 28, but most traders expect another hike by December, with US inflation at 3.7%.
beats.happened: Spot gold traded near $3,995, down about 0.5%, and silver near $52.75, down about 2%. Oil stayed high on tension around the Strait of Hormuz, the 10-year US Treasury yield sat near 4.98%, and the dollar was firm. Silver fell more on worries about factory demand.
beats.means: In this war, high oil is working against gold: it feeds inflation, which keeps the Fed leaning toward hikes and outweighs gold's role as a shelter.
beats.fx: High oil → sticky US inflation → odds of a Fed hike stay high → pressure on gold.

impact.why: Firm dollar, high yields and Fed hike bets pull gold back under $4,000.
The same hike bets keep the dollar firm.

items.watch: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's tone on Wednesday and Thursday's US PCE inflation figure.

items.headline: US Durable Goods Orders Rise 1.8%, but Aircraft Drive Much of the Strength
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: Orders for long-lasting US goods rose 1.8% in September, more than expected, but a jump in aircraft orders did most of the work. Orders that track business investment grew more slowly than in August.

beats.was: The US Federal Reserve decides on rates on Wednesday, October 28, and is expected to hold; markets mostly expect a hike in December, so each US figure this week is read for how strong the economy still is.
beats.happened: The Census Bureau's early report showed new orders for durable goods, things built to last three years or more, rose 1.8% in September to about $345 billion, helped by a 28% jump in orders for civilian aircraft. Leaving out transport, orders rose 0.5%, a little under forecasts. Orders for business equipment outside aircraft and defence rose 0.5%, slower than August's 1.6%, though shipments of that equipment picked up.
beats.means: Factories are still getting more orders, which fits a US economy that is holding up. But plane orders are lumpy, and the steadier business-investment measure cooled, so this adds little to the case for a December hike.
beats.fx: Bigger headline orders → a little more support for higher US rates → mild help for the dollar; softer core orders → that help stays small.

impact.why: Headline orders beat, though aircraft drove it and business-equipment orders slowed.

items.watch: Whether Thursday's US inflation figure and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's words on Wednesday firm up or cool the December hike bets.

items.headline: Iran's supreme leader calls for meeting Tehran's conditions to end war
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said on Tuesday the war can end only if the conditions set by Iran's officials are met, and stressed keeping control of the Strait of Hormuz. Oil slipped as traders read it as Tehran talking about terms, not walking away.

beats.was: Iran has been at war with the US since February, and the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of the world's energy before the war, is running at around 60% of normal flows. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday and agreed to keep talking.
beats.happened: Khamenei met Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, and said Iran's terms for ending the war must be met and the current 'neither war nor peace' state brought to an end. He also stressed managing the Strait of Hormuz and closer ties with neighbours. Oil prices slipped about 1% on the day, with US crude near $101.
beats.means: Iran's top leader is talking about how the war ends, which supports the diplomacy of the past few days. But he set no new offer and repeated that Iran wants its own conditions met, including a say over Hormuz, so a deal is not close.
beats.fx: Talk of ending the war → less fear of lost supply → lower oil, a small help for oil importers like Japan and the euro area; no concession on Hormuz → the supply risk stays.

impact.why: Iran's leader frames terms for ending the war, adding to the diplomacy that has pulled prices off their highs.
Lower oil trims Canada's export income.
Cheaper oil helps Japan's import bill, but calmer nerves cut demand for shelter.

items.watch: Whether the US answers Iran's terms, or new attacks on ships near Hormuz or on Saudi oil sites push the talks back.

items.headline: Houthis accuse Egypt of 'declaring war' by backing Saudi Arabia
items.story_title: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and who joins the defence
items.summary: Egypt's parliament has allowed President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to send military help to Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. A senior Houthi leader called it a declaration of war on Yemen.

beats.was: Yemen's Houthi movement, allied with Iran, has fired missiles and drones at Saudi oil sites, airports and cities for weeks, including a claimed hit on the big Ras Tanura refinery on Tuesday. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan already have a defence pact, and Britain has sent fighter jets.
beats.happened: In a closed session on Monday, at least two thirds of Egypt's lawmakers authorised Sisi to take whatever steps are needed to help Saudi Arabia defend itself. No troops have been sent yet and Saudi Arabia has not made a formal request. Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthis' political leadership, said Egypt had in effect declared war on Yemen.
beats.means: The fight around Saudi Arabia is drawing in more countries, which raises the chance it lasts longer. Egypt also runs the Suez Canal, so a wider clash near the Red Sea is a risk for shipping, though no threat to shipping has been made.
beats.fx: A wider war around Saudi oil sites → a bigger risk premium in oil → support for oil-linked currencies like the loonie and more demand for shelter like the franc.

impact.why: More countries joining raises the risk to Saudi supply, but no troops have moved yet.
Talk of a wider war adds a little to demand for shelter.

items.watch: Whether Egyptian forces actually go to Saudi Arabia, and how the Houthis respond.

items.headline: OPEC+ oil producers set to keep output targets steady at Sunday meeting, sources say
items.story_title: Iran war: the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Seven core OPEC+ oil producers, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, are expected to keep December output targets unchanged at an online meeting on Sunday, November 1, three sources told Reuters.

beats.was: The Iran war cut Gulf oil exports for months and pushed Brent above $110 a barrel. OPEC+ finished undoing one layer of output cuts in September.
beats.happened: Sources said no final decision has been made, but the group is unlikely to change policy before next year. Most Gulf members are pumping well below their targets anyway as they rebuild exports after the war disruption. A review of how much each member can produce, which sets 2027 targets, is expected in mid-November.
beats.means: The targets are not what limits supply right now; the war is. A steady decision would leave oil prices to follow the Gulf fighting and peace talks.
beats.fx: No change in targets → no new push on oil → oil-linked currencies like the Canadian dollar keep following war headlines instead.

impact.why: An expected hold from unnamed sources; supply is set by the war, not the targets.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, November 1.

items.headline: Japan's trend inflation index hits 3-year high, cements case for BOJ rate hike
items.story_title: Bank of Japan: hold now, hike later?
items.summary: A Bank of Japan measure of underlying inflation rose to 3.2% in September, its fastest in three years. It strengthens the case for another rate rise after Friday's meeting, where the bank is expected to hold.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan's rate is 1.25%, far below US rates, which keeps the yen weak near 158 per dollar. The bank says it sets the pace of hikes by underlying inflation, not by swings in energy or one-off government subsidies.
beats.happened: The bank's own gauge that strips out those one-off factors rose 3.2% from a year earlier in September, up from 2.6% in August and the biggest rise since October 2023. Prices companies charge each other for services also stayed high, pushed up by soaring shipping costs, a weak yen and dearer imported fuel.
beats.means: Price rises are spreading through the economy, which is what the bank wants to see before it raises rates again. A hold this Friday with a clear hint about December looks more likely.
beats.fx: Firmer underlying inflation → more chance of a December Bank of Japan hike → narrower gap with US rates → some support for the yen.

impact.why: Broadening inflation supports a later Bank of Japan hike, though Friday's hold is expected.

items.watch: Friday's Bank of Japan decision and Governor Kazuo Ueda's press conference: a clear signal for December would help the yen; no hint would leave it weak.
